mediator

/MEE-dee-ay-ter/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A mediator is a neutral third party who helps two sides in a dispute reach their own agreement.

The strike ended only after a federal mediator got the airline and the union back to the same table.

Example

Neither brother would speak to the other about their late father's hardware store, so the family hired a mediator. She had no power to award the store to anyone — but by the second session she had each brother pricing the other's plan, and by Friday they had drawn up a buyout both could sign.

A mediator stands in the middle of a dispute and belongs to neither side. The word insists on two limits: neutrality — a mediator argues for no one — and restraint — unlike a judge or an arbitrator, a mediator decides nothing. The parties keep the power; the mediator keeps them talking.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

go-between: A go-between carries messages across a divide and stops there. A mediator does more than ferry words — a mediator steers the two sides toward a settlement they write themselves.

peacemaker: A peacemaker is anyone who tries to end a quarrel, by any means and from any position — even from inside the fight. A mediator works from a precise spot: outside the dispute, neutral, and welcome to both sides.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

partisan: someone firmly attached to one side of the fight

instigator: someone who stirs the quarrel up rather than settling it

Where it sits · how much power over the outcome the third party holds

go-between → mediator → arbitrator

go-between vs. mediator: A go-between is weaker than a mediator: carrying messages across the divide is the whole job, while a mediator actively works the two sides toward a settlement.

arbitrator vs. mediator: An arbitrator goes further than a mediator — a mediator guides the talks but decides nothing, while an arbitrator hears both sides and hands down a ruling that binds them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — medi-: middle (Latin medius)

Suffix — -ator: one who does

Put it together: Medi- (middle) + -ator (one who does) = one who works the middle. Latin mediare meant to stand at the midpoint, halving the distance between two ends. A mediator still earns the name literally: planted between two sides, belonging to neither, working the middle ground until the sides can meet on it.

Use the root in a new word: intermediate: Only the intermediate slopes were open after the storm, so everyone skied them.

Word Choice

neutral / procedural — courtrooms, contracts, diplomacy

Mediator is the word courts, unions, and diplomats use for the neutral in the middle — precise about both neutrality and limits. If the third party rules, say arbitrator or judge; if they argue one side, say advocate. And keep the sound-alike straight: mediation settles disputes; meditation is what you do on a quiet cushion.
